title: Some and Any in Food Contexts
description: Master the rules of 'some' and 'any' across affirmative, negative, questions, and polite offers.
objectives: Use 'some' in affirmative statements with plural countable and uncountable nouns
Use 'any' in negative statements and general questions
Apply the crucial exception: use 'some' in polite offers and requests (Would you like some tea?)

sections.title: The Standard Rules for Some & Any
sections.content:
Both **some** and **any** mean an unspecified amount or number. They are used with **plural countable nouns** (*apples*) and **uncountable nouns** (*milk*).

### 1. Affirmative Statements: Use SOME
- *There is **some** milk in the fridge.*
- *We have **some** fresh apples on the table.*

### 2. Negative Statements: Use ANY
- *There isn't **any** milk left.*
- *We don't have **any** apples today.*

### 3. General Questions: Use ANY
- *Is there **any** tea in the pot?*
- *Do you have **any** brothers?*

### 4. The Polite Offer / Request Exception: Use SOME
When offering something politely or asking for something where you expect a 'yes', use **SOME**, not any:
- *Would you like **some** tea?* (Offer)
- *Can I have **some** water, please?* (Request)

callouts.title: Hospitality Rule
callouts.text: When serving guests, always say: **Would you like some tea / some biscuits?** Using 'any' in an offer can sound cold or skeptical.

callouts.title: Never with Singular Countable Nouns
callouts.text: Do NOT use some/any for one countable item. Say **an apple**, NOT *'some apple'*.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
summaryPoints: Use 'some' in positive statements (There is some milk).
Use 'any' in negative statements (There isn't any milk).
Use 'any' in general questions (Is there any milk?).
EXCEPTION: Use 'some' for polite offers (Would you like some tea?) and requests (Can I have some water?).
Both words work with uncountable nouns and plural countable nouns.
